## Candidate 01 — Total Internal Reflection: Refracted Ray Sweeping to 90° Then Vanishing

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/02-reflection-refraction.md`
- Topic: Total internal reflection · critical angle
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The refracted ray doesn't gradually dim — it physically disappears at a precise angle, and the moment it vanishes is the same moment all the light reverses back into the glass. Watching it happen is more convincing than any diagram.
- The rule: Snell's law n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ with θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁). For θ₁ > θ_c, no real solution exists for θ₂ and the refracted ray ceases to exist.
- Concrete numbers: Glass-to-air: n₁=1.5, n₂=1.0 → θ_c = arcsin(2/3) ≈ 41.8°. Scripted incident angle sequence: 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°, 41°, 41.8° (TIR onset), 45°, 60°. Diamond case: n₁=2.42 → θ_c≈24.4° (shown as contrast beat). Fiber-optic worked example: n_core=1.62, n_clad=1.52 → θ_c≈69.8°.
- The artifact / what moves: A glass-air interface drawn horizontally. An incident ray (orange) descends at increasing angles through the scripted sequence. The refracted ray (green) below the interface sweeps from nearly vertical up toward 90° (grazing), then at θ=θ_c the green ray reaches 90° and lies flat along the interface — then at the next step angle it vanishes entirely, replaced by a strong reflected ray (blue) that brightens visibly. The critical angle value is annotated live.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At θ₁=41.8° for glass-to-air (n₁=1.5, n₂=1.0), θ₂=arcsin(1.5×sin41.8°/1.0)=arcsin(0.999)≈90° — the refracted ray grazes the interface. P2: For n₁=2.42 (diamond), θ_c=arcsin(1/2.42)=24.4° — TIR onset at less than 25° incidence, meaning most internal light reflects back without escape, verifiable from Snell's law.
- The change: Animate the fiber-optic geometry — show a ray bouncing down a cylindrical fiber via repeated TIR reflections at the core-cladding boundary (n_core=1.62, n_clad=1.52), demonstrating why fiber optics work.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: TIR is not a failure of Snell's law — it is Snell's law having no real solution. The animation reveals that the critical angle is the boundary between "Snell's law solvable" and "Snell's law has no answer."
- Exclusions: Do not animate evanescent waves (beyond intro scope); do not show Fresnel reflection coefficients.
- Sim slug: total-internal-reflection-sweep
- Score: 10/10

## Candidate 02 — Single-Slit Sinc² Pattern Drawing: Width Inverting as Slit Narrows

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/06-diffraction.md`
- Topic: Single-slit diffraction · sinc² envelope
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: Make the slit half as wide and the central maximum doubles in width — the artifact that diffracts least is the one that spreads most, which is backwards from every geometric-optics instinct.
- The rule: I(θ) = I₀[sin(α)/α]² where α = πa·sinθ/λ. Minima at a·sinθ = mλ. Central maximum full-width = 2λ/a.
- Concrete numbers: λ=550nm. Scripted slit-width sequence: a=0.5mm (central max half-angle=0.063°), a=0.2mm (0.158°), a=0.1mm (0.315°), a=0.05mm (0.63°). Verify: a=0.1mm first minimum at sinθ=λ/a=550e-9/1e-4=0.0055 rad. Side lobes at a·sinθ=2λ, 3λ,... with intensities 4.7%, 1.7% of central maximum.
- The artifact / what moves: An intensity pattern drawn as a bright horizontal band on a "screen," computed from the sinc² formula. As the slit width decreases through the scripted sequence, the central maximum widens, the side lobes spread further apart, and the peak intensity falls (area is conserved). The drawing happens in real-time — the pattern sweeps outward from center as if the light were diffusing. A live label shows current a and central-maximum width.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At a=0.1mm and λ=500nm, first minimum occurs at sinθ=λ/a=0.005 rad (0.287°) — verifiable by computing α=π×0.1e-3×0.005/500e-9 = π, where sinc²(π)=0. P2: The intensity at the first-order side lobe maximum (at α≈3π/2) is I/I₀=[sin(3π/2)/(3π/2)]²=1/(3π/2)²≈0.045 = 4.5% of central maximum — checkable against the formula.
- The change: Add the double-slit compound pattern: show the sinc² diffraction envelope and the cosine-squared interference fringes multiplied together, with the first interference null coinciding with the diffraction minimum (when d/a is an integer).
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Geometric optics says smaller aperture = sharper image; wave optics says smaller aperture = wider diffraction. The animation shows exactly where geometric optics fails and wave optics takes over.
- Exclusions: Do not animate Huygens wavelet construction (too slow for this format); do not show near-field (Fresnel) diffraction.
- Sim slug: single-slit-diffraction-sinc-squared
- Score: 10/10

## Candidate 03 — Snell's Law Geometry: Ray Bending as n₂/n₁ Ratio Sweeps

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/02-reflection-refraction.md`
- Topic: Snell's law · refraction geometry
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The same angle of incidence produces bending toward the normal in one direction and away from it in the other — depending on which side is denser. Watching the ray reverse its bend direction as n₂/n₁ crosses 1 makes the law feel like geometry rather than a formula.
- The rule: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂. θ₂ = arcsin(n₁/n₂ × sinθ₁).
- Concrete numbers: Fixed incident angle θ₁=45°. Scripted n₂/n₁ ratio sequence: 0.5 (glass-to-air direction), 0.75, 1.0 (no bending), 1.33 (air-to-water), 1.5 (air-to-glass), 2.42 (air-to-diamond). At n₁=1.0, n₂=1.5, θ₁=45°: θ₂=arcsin(sin45°/1.5)=arcsin(0.471)=28.1°. Full Brewster's angle beat: at n₂/n₁=1.5, θ_B=arctan(1.5)≈56.3°.
- The artifact / what moves: A flat interface with incident ray fixed at 45°. The refracted ray animates smoothly as n₂/n₁ sweeps from 0.5 to 2.42 — below 1 the ray bends away from the normal and approaches TIR, at 1 it passes straight through, above 1 it bends toward the normal and compresses. The normal line is drawn as a fixed reference; angle labels θ₁ and θ₂ update in real-time with numerical values.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At n₁=1.0, n₂=1.5, θ₁=30°: θ₂=arcsin(sin30°/1.5)=arcsin(0.333)=19.47° — refracted ray closer to normal, verifiable from Snell's law. P2: At n₁=1.5, n₂=1.0, θ₁=45°: θ₂=arcsin(1.5×sin45°)=arcsin(1.06) — no real solution, TIR occurs at this angle because θ₁=45°>θ_c=41.8°.
- The change: Add the Brewster's angle beat — as θ₁ sweeps from 0° to 90° for n₁=1, n₂=1.5, mark the angle where the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular (θ_B=56.3°), showing the geometric condition that kills p-polarized reflection.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Snell's law is a consequence of wavefronts matching across the boundary, not a fact about rays — the animation teaches the law without explaining why it holds, which is intentional at this level.
- Exclusions: Do not animate polarization components; do not animate Fresnel coefficient magnitudes.
- Sim slug: snells-law-geometry-sweep
- Score: 9/10

## Candidate 04 — Double-Slit Interference: Fringe Pattern Drawing as d Changes

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/05-interference.md`
- Topic: Young's double-slit experiment · fringe spacing
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: Doubling the slit separation halves the fringe spacing — and watching the fringes compress as d increases makes the counter-intuitive relationship (more separated sources → finer fringes) stick permanently.
- The rule: I(θ) = I₀cos²(πd·sinθ/λ). Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d. Bright fringes at y = mλL/d.
- Concrete numbers: λ=550nm, L=1.0m. Scripted d sequence: d=0.05mm (Δy=11mm), d=0.1mm (Δy=5.5mm), d=0.2mm (Δy=2.75mm), d=0.5mm (Δy=1.1mm), d=1.0mm (Δy=0.55mm). Verify: at λ=633nm, d=0.2mm, L=1m, Δy=633e-9×1/2e-4=3.16mm.
- The artifact / what moves: Two slits on the left, a vertical screen on the right at distance L. The interference pattern draws as alternating bright and dark vertical bands on the screen. As d increases through the scripted sequence, the bands compress — visibly more fringes fitting in the same screen height. A live label shows current d and computed Δy. The animation also shows the path-length difference geometry with two rays drawn from the slits converging to a point on the screen.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At d=0.1mm, λ=550nm, L=1m, fringe spacing Δy=λL/d=5.5mm — measurable by counting fringes in the animation against a scale bar. P2: At λ=633nm (red) vs λ=405nm (violet) with same d and L, red fringes are 633/405≈1.56× wider than violet — verifiable from the Δy formula.
- The change: Increase N slits from 2 to 10 while holding d and λ fixed — the principal maxima remain at the same positions but sharpen dramatically (narrower peak width ∝ 1/N), transitioning from double-slit to grating regime.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: More separation between sources produces finer fringes — the animation enforces this anti-intuitive fact by making the compression visible and measurable.
- Exclusions: Do not animate wavefront propagation or Huygens sources; do not include diffraction envelope modulation (save for candidate 02's compound pattern beat).
- Sim slug: double-slit-interference-fringe-spacing
- Score: 9/10

## Candidate 05 — Thin-Lens Image Position: 1/d_i Tracing a Reciprocal Curve as Object Moves

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/04-lenses.md`
- Topic: Thin-lens equation · image formation geometry
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: At the focal length the image jumps to infinity, then reappears on the same side as the object as a virtual image — and watching this discontinuity happen during a smooth sweep of object distance is one of those moments where geometric optics becomes genuinely surprising.
- The rule: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i → d_i = f·d_o/(d_o − f). Magnification m = −d_i/d_o. Real image when d_i>0; virtual when d_i<0.
- Concrete numbers: Converging lens f=10cm. Scripted d_o sequence: 50cm (d_i=12.5cm, m=−0.25 real inverted reduced), 20cm (d_i=20cm, m=−1.0 real inverted same-size), 15cm (d_i=30cm, m=−2.0 real inverted enlarged), 10.1cm (d_i≈1010cm, m≈−100 near-infinity), 10cm (no image), 8cm (d_i=−40cm, m=+5 virtual upright enlarged, makeup-mirror case), 5cm (d_i=−10cm, m=+2).
- The artifact / what moves: Three principal rays drawn from the tip of an object arrow through a thin lens. As d_o decreases through the scripted sequence, the three rays animate — the image point traces rightward toward infinity (as d_o approaches f), then jumps to the left side of the lens as virtual. The image arrow flips from inverted-small to virtual-upright-large, and numerical readouts show live d_i and m values. The lens is drawn as a vertical line with converging symbol.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At d_o=20cm with f=10cm, d_i=f·d_o/(d_o−f)=10×20/10=20cm and m=−1 — the image is the same size as the object, inverted, at 2f from the lens. P2: At d_o=8cm with f=10cm (object inside focal length), d_i=10×8/(8−10)=80/(−2)=−40cm (virtual, same side as object) and m=−(−40)/8=+5 — upright, 5× enlarged — verifiable from the thin-lens formula.
- The change: Switch to a diverging lens (f=−10cm) — show that d_i is always negative (always virtual) regardless of d_o, and m is always between 0 and 1 (always reduced), making the "convex mirror" analogy explicit.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The thin-lens equation is a hyperbola in (d_o, d_i) space — the animation traces that hyperbola by moving the object, making the algebraic singularity at d_o=f into a geometric event.
- Exclusions: Do not animate chromatic aberration or spherical aberration; do not show lensmaker's equation derivation.
- Sim slug: thin-lens-image-position-sweep
- Score: 9/10

## Candidate 06 — Fabry-Pérot Resonance: Cavity Mode Lines Sharpening as N Increases

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/09-coherence-lasers.md`
- Topic: Laser cavity modes · Fabry-Pérot resonator
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: A cavity that is 30cm long selects discrete frequency slots 500MHz apart — and as the gain bandwidth slides over those slots, you can count exactly how many modes lase simultaneously. The discreteness feels like an algorithm choosing frequencies, not a continuous physical process.
- The rule: Cavity resonance condition: L = mλ/2 → ν_m = mc/(2L). Mode spacing Δν = c/(2L). Number of lasing modes = gain bandwidth / Δν.
- Concrete numbers: L=30cm → Δν=500MHz. Gain bandwidth: HeNe ≈ 1.5GHz → 3 lasing modes. Scripted L sequence: 10cm (Δν=1.5GHz, 1 mode), 30cm (500MHz, 3 modes), 60cm (250MHz, 6 modes), 100cm (150MHz, 10 modes). Gaussian beam waist at λ=633nm, w₀=1mm: z_R = π×(10⁻³)²/(633e-9) ≈ 4.96m.
- The artifact / what moves: A frequency axis showing the gain profile as a Gaussian envelope (fixed width 1.5GHz). Cavity mode lines drawn as sharp vertical spikes spaced by c/(2L). As L increases through the scripted sequence, the spike spacing decreases — more spikes fit under the gain envelope. Each spike within the envelope brightens (the lasing modes). A live counter shows "N lasing modes = X." The Gaussian beam profile w(z) draws in a second panel below, showing the beam waist and divergence for the same cavity length.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At L=30cm, Δν=c/(2L)=3e8/(0.6)=5e8 Hz=500MHz — and 1.5GHz/500MHz=3 modes within the gain bandwidth — verifiable by the chapter's worked example. P2: At L=10cm, Δν=1.5GHz exactly equals the gain bandwidth — so only 1 mode (or barely 1) fits under the envelope, approaching single-mode operation — verifiable from the formula.
- The change: Add an etalon filter (narrow transmission peak 50MHz wide) inside the cavity — show how it selects exactly one cavity mode even in a 100cm cavity, visually showing how mode selection works in precision lasers.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The cavity is not a container — it is a filter. The animation reveals that lasing is the intersection of "what the gain medium can amplify" and "what the cavity allows to resonate."
- Exclusions: Do not animate stimulated emission at the atomic level; do not animate Gaussian beam propagation through external optics.
- Sim slug: fabry-perot-cavity-modes
- Score: 9/10

## Candidate 07 — Dispersion in a Prism: White Light Splitting Wavelength by Wavelength

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/02-reflection-refraction.md`
- Topic: Dispersion · wavelength-dependent refraction
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: Red and violet enter a prism as one beam and exit as two — but the 1.7° angular separation between them comes entirely from a refractive index difference of only 0.017. The animation makes visible how small an index difference compounds across two refractions into a visible rainbow.
- The rule: n(λ) = A + B/λ² (Cauchy). For glass: A≈1.5, B≈0.01µm². Snell's law applied twice at prism surfaces; apex angle α; angle of minimum deviation δ_min.
- Concrete numbers: Prism apex angle α=60°, angle of incidence θ₁=50°. n_red=1.515 → θ₂_red=arcsin(sin50°/1.515)=arcsin(0.505)=30.35°; exit angle=arcsin(1.515×sin(60°−30.35°))=arcsin(1.515×sin29.65°)=arcsin(0.749)≈48.5°. n_violet=1.532 → θ₂_violet=arcsin(sin50°/1.532)=arcsin(0.499)=29.97°; exit angle≈49.2°. Angular separation: 49.2°−48.5°=0.7° (for this configuration; chapter quotes similar calculation).
- The artifact / what moves: A triangular glass prism drawn center-screen. A single white beam enters the left face. Inside the prism, it separates into a fan of rays from deep red (700nm) to violet (400nm), each computed from the Cauchy formula. The rays exit the right face and diverge into a visible spectrum. The animation draws each wavelength's path in sequence from red to violet, with the current wavelength and refractive index labeled. The final frame shows all rays together as a rainbow fan.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: For glass with A=1.5, B=0.01µm², n at 700nm = 1.5+0.01/0.49≈1.520; n at 400nm = 1.5+0.01/0.16≈1.563 — a difference of 0.043 — verifiable from the Cauchy formula. P2: For the exercise in the chapter (α=60°, θ₁=50°, n_red=1.515, n_violet=1.532), angular separation between red and violet after the prism exit ≈0.7° — verifiable by applying Snell's law twice for each wavelength.
- The change: Animate the rainbow formation — show parallel sun rays entering individual spherical water droplets, refracting in, internally reflecting once, refracting out, with red exiting at 42° and violet at 40° from the anti-solar point, building the rainbow geometry.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: A rainbow and a prism are the same equation applied to different geometry — the animation makes the refractive index difference of 0.04 produce a 2° angular separation in the sky, which is why the rainbow has width.
- Exclusions: Do not animate secondary rainbow (requires two internal reflections — beyond intro scope); do not animate polarization of rainbow light.
- Sim slug: prism-dispersion-white-light

## Candidate 08 — Rayleigh Criterion: Two Airy Disks Merging as Angular Separation Shrinks

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/06-diffraction.md`; `physics-optics/chapters/08-optical-instruments.md`
- Topic: Rayleigh criterion · diffraction-limited resolution
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: The moment two stars merge into one is not arbitrary — it is exactly when the maximum of one Airy pattern sits on the first minimum of the other. Watching the two disks slide together to that precise moment gives the abstract formula a concrete visual threshold.
- The rule: θ_min = 1.22λ/D (Rayleigh criterion). Two point sources just resolved when their Airy-pattern maxima are separated by 1.22λ/D radians.
- Concrete numbers: D=100mm aperture, λ=550nm → θ_min=1.22×5.5e-7/0.1=6.71µrad=1.38 arcsec. Hubble (D=2.4m): θ_min=0.058 arcsec. JWST (D=6.5m): θ_min=0.021 arcsec. Scripted angular separation sequence: 5×θ_min (clearly resolved), 2×θ_min, θ_min (Rayleigh limit), 0.5×θ_min (unresolved).
- The artifact / what moves: Two identical Airy disk intensity patterns (bright central core with ring halos) displayed side by side. As the scripted angular separation decreases, the two disks slide toward each other — at θ_min, the outer edges of the central disks just touch and the gap between them is barely distinguishable. Below θ_min, they merge into a single elongated blob. A live label shows the current separation in units of θ_min and the aperture diameter.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At θ=θ_min=1.22λ/D, the first minimum of one Airy pattern falls exactly on the maximum of the other — the two centers are separated by 1.22λ/D radians and the combined pattern shows a just-perceptible saddle between the two peaks (intensity dip to 73.5% of peak). P2: A 2.4m aperture (Hubble) resolves 6.5/2.4≈2.7× finer than a 6.5m aperture (JWST) would at the same wavelength — the Rayleigh limit scales as 1/D.
- The change: Animate a telescope aperture doubling from 100mm to 200mm — the Airy disks shrink by half and previously-merged sources re-separate, showing why larger aperture = better resolution.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The Rayleigh criterion is a convention, not a law — but the saddle point it defines is an objective feature of the pattern. The animation shows the saddle appearing and disappearing as a function of separation.
- Exclusions: Do not animate the Bessel function derivation; do not include adaptive optics discussion.
- Sim slug: rayleigh-criterion-airy-disk-merge

## Candidate 09 — Brewster's Angle: Reflected Intensity Falling to Zero for p-Polarization

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/02-reflection-refraction.md`; `physics-optics/chapters/07-polarization.md`
- Topic: Brewster's angle · polarization by reflection
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: At one precise angle of incidence, the p-polarized component of reflected light disappears entirely — but the s-polarized component doesn't. This asymmetry is why a polarized sunglass lens can black out glare from a road puddle while leaving the sky visible.
- The rule: θ_B = arctan(n₂/n₁). At θ_B, reflected p-polarization = 0. Fresnell coefficient r_p = (n₂cosθ₁ − n₁cosθ₂)/(n₂cosθ₁ + n₁cosθ₂) = 0 when reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.
- Concrete numbers: Air-to-glass: n₁=1.0, n₂=1.5 → θ_B=arctan(1.5)≈56.3°. At θ_B: the reflected ray and refracted ray are perpendicular (θ_r + θ_t = 90°, verifiable: θ_t = arcsin(sin56.3°/1.5)=arcsin(0.554)=33.7°; 56.3°+33.7°=90°). Scripted θ₁ sweep: 0° to 89° in 15° steps plus θ_B=56.3°.
- The artifact / what moves: A glass surface. An incident ray with two labeled polarization components (p: in plane of incidence, s: perpendicular). As θ₁ sweeps from 0° to 90°, two intensity curves (one for r_p², one for r_s²) are plotted in a corner panel — r_s² decreases monotonically, but r_p² dips to zero at θ_B then rises again. At the moment θ₁=56.3°, the p-polarized reflected ray visually disappears (the p-component label dims to zero) while the s-component remains — the geometry shows reflected+refracted rays exactly 90° apart.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At θ_B=arctan(n₂/n₁)=arctan(1.5)=56.3° for air-glass, the refracted angle is 33.7° and the two rays are perpendicular — 56.3°+33.7°=90°, verifiable by Snell's law. P2: For water (n=1.33), θ_B=arctan(1.33)=53.06° — horizontal puddles produce fully s-polarized reflected glare at this angle, which polarizing sunglasses (horizontal axis blocked) eliminate — verifiable from the formula.
- The change: Animate θ_B changing as n₂ increases from 1.0 to 2.4 — showing Brewster's angle sweeping from 45° (n=1) to 67° (n=2.4) as material density increases.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: Polarizing sunglasses are an application of a geometric accident — the reflected and refracted rays happen to be perpendicular at one specific angle, which kills the p-component. The animation shows the geometry that produces this accident.
- Exclusions: Do not animate the Fresnel coefficient derivation; do not include circular polarization analysis.
- Sim slug: brewsters-angle-polarization
- Score: 8/10

## Candidate 10 — Gaussian Beam: Waist-Divergence Trade-Off Drawing as w₀ Decreases

- Source: `physics-optics/chapters/09-coherence-lasers.md`
- Topic: Gaussian beam · diffraction-limited propagation
- Lane: MANIM (directed animation)
- Hook: Focusing a laser beam tighter makes it diverge faster — and there is a fundamental product w₀×θ_div = λ/π that cannot be beaten. Watching the beam envelope pinch and then flare faster as w₀ shrinks makes the Heisenberg-like constraint in optics feel physical.
- The rule: w(z) = w₀√(1+(z/z_R)²) where z_R = πw₀²/λ. Divergence θ_div ≈ λ/(πw₀). Product: w₀×θ_div = λ/π (constant for fixed λ).
- Concrete numbers: λ=633nm (HeNe). Scripted w₀ sequence: 2mm (z_R=19.8m, θ_div=0.10mrad), 1mm (z_R=4.96m, 0.20mrad), 0.5mm (z_R=1.24m, 0.40mrad), 0.1mm (z_R=0.050m, 2.0mrad). At z=z_R, w(z)=w₀√2≈1.41×w₀ always (universal ratio independent of w₀ or λ).
- The artifact / what moves: A beam profile w(z) plotted as two symmetric curves (upper and lower envelopes of the Gaussian beam). The beam narrowest at z=0 (the waist). As w₀ decreases through the scripted sequence, the waist becomes narrower but the Rayleigh range shrinks dramatically and the divergence angle widens — the two envelope curves open outward faster. A live label shows current w₀, z_R, and θ_div. The product w₀×θ_div is displayed as a constant (λ/π≈201nm) across all cases.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At w₀=1mm and λ=633nm, z_R=π×(10⁻³)²/(6.33e-7)≈4.97m — verifiable from the formula; the beam stays within √2×w₀ for ±4.97m. P2: At z=z_R (one Rayleigh range from the waist), beam radius w=w₀√2 regardless of the value of w₀ or λ — a universal geometric ratio baked into the beam equation.
- The change: Change wavelength from 633nm (visible) to 10.6µm (CO₂ laser) at fixed w₀=1mm — show z_R shrinking by a factor of 16.7 (proportional to 1/λ), beam divergence increasing by 16.7×, demonstrating why infrared industrial lasers must be focused much closer to the workpiece.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The waist-divergence product is the optical analogue of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle — position and momentum cannot both be zero. The animation reveals this constraint as a geometric fact about Gaussian beams, not a quantum mystery.
- Exclusions: Do not animate higher-order (TEM₀₁, etc.) Gaussian modes; do not include the Guoy phase shift.
- Sim slug: gaussian-beam-waist-divergence
- Score: 7/10

- The rule: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i; m = −d_i/d_o. For concave mirror f>0: real inverted image when d_o>f, virtual upright when d_o<f.
- Concrete numbers: f=15cm (makeup mirror scenario from chapter). Scripted d_o sequence: 45cm (d_i=22.5cm, m=−0.5 real reduced inverted), 30cm (d_i=30cm, m=−1 real same-size), 20cm (d_i=60cm, m=−3 real enlarged inverted), 15cm (d_i→∞), 12cm (d_i=−60cm, m=+5 virtual upright enlarged), 8cm (d_i=−24cm, m=+3).
- The artifact / what moves: Three principal rays drawn from the tip of an object arrow to a concave mirror, with reflections following the focal-ray and parallel-ray rules. As d_o decreases through the scripted sequence, the reflected rays shift — the image point moves rightward, reaches the focal plane (rays go parallel), then the image appears on the same side as the object (virtual). The image arrow flips from inverted to upright as d_o crosses f. Live readouts: d_i, m, image type.
- Output medium: Manim (mp4)
- Two testable predictions: P1: At d_o=20cm with f=15cm, d_i=15×20/(20−15)=60cm and m=−60/20=−3 — real, inverted, 3× enlarged — verifiable from the mirror equation. P2: At d_o=12cm with f=15cm, d_i=15×12/(12−15)=180/(−3)=−60cm (virtual) and m=−(−60)/12=+5 — virtual, upright, 5× enlarged — the makeup-mirror scenario.
- The change: Switch to a convex mirror (f=−15cm) — show that d_i is always negative (always virtual) and m always between 0 and 1 (always reduced), regardless of d_o, demonstrating why convex mirrors provide wide-angle views.
- Human supplies (Claude can't): Nothing — fully synthetic/analytic
- Teardown angle: The focal point is not where images form — it is the dividing line between two different image regimes. The animation shows the transition by making the object cross that line.
- Exclusions: Do not animate spherical aberration; do not include parabolic mirror correction.
